articles.title: Searching for past glory
articles.content: THE collective memory of Muslim societies, particularly in the West and South Asia, is based on the persistent idea that since the collapse of the Ottoman Empire they have been in need of a joint response to challenges ranging from politics to defence. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia may be seen as something of a pioneer on this front with the creation of the Islamic Military Alliance to Fight Terrorism in 2015, which was partly the basis for the recently concludedMakkah Joint Defence Agreement. However, Pakistan has always championed such ambitions. The roots go much further back, with the Baghdad Pact representing an important milestone in that journey. The concept of a collective Muslim response has been conceived and framed in different ways, from the idea of the ummah to its more structured institutional expression within the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. Its character has continued to evolve as changing political objectives have redirected the ideological orientation of Muslim states. In Pakistan’s case, however, this idea has shaped not only the country’s ideology but also its internal politics and models of state structure. There is little doubt that Pakistan’s growing role in the Gulf, beginning with Trump’sGaza peace plan, followed by theIslamabad MoUand now the Makkah accord, has boosted the country’s confidence. However, when its leadership looks inward at the political and economic conditions, the contrast undermines some of the confidence gained from its successes in an evolving geopolitical environment. This disparity frustrates the power elite, that wants to address internal problems immediately and sustain the country’s momentum in the external arena. To achieve internal stability and order comparable to that in Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, Pakistan’s other regional partners, the power elite here appears prepared to take several political risks. These could include major administrative engineering, such as thecreation of new provinces, a step that would come at considerable political cost. Pakistan is deepening its West Asian ties to bolster its defence power and strategic weight. This argument is not intended to evaluate the costs and benefits of creating new provinces. Rather, it seeks to trace the trigger that makes the power elite nervous when its external successes do not correspond with domestic political realities and the state of the economy. There can be several interpretations of this contradiction, ranging from the political economy to the changing geopolitical order. Yet an important dimension is often missing from the debate: the triangle of ideology, statecraft and geography. Pakistan and Turkiye share a geographical anxiety: their military power and ambitions do not fully correspond with the territories they control, while their opportunities for geographical expansion are extremely limited. This creates a middle-power anxiety about sustaining and enhancing their military and defence capabilities. Both countries are responding to this challenge in their own ways. Turkiye is pursuing regional groupings, alliances and transnational Turkic partnerships. Pakistan, meanwhile, appears to be abandoning its old strategy of ‘strategic depth’ or the attempt to expand its influence to neighbouring territories to overcome its geographical anxieties. Instead, it is engaging more deeply in West Asia to strengthen its defence capabilities and strategic weight. The purpose is obvious: Pakistan faces a much larger geographical and military power in India. Saudi Arabia faces a different middle-power dilemma. Its primary concerns are sustaining economic stability and protecting itself from regional forces that it perceives as ideologically hostile or hegemonically ambitious, principally Iran and Israel. Saudi Arabia has learned to coexist with Israel, but Israel’s hegemonic ambitions continue to generate anxiety about the future regional order. Riyadh is also concerned about hostile forces near its borders, particularly in Yemen, where Iran has effectively projected its influence. Pakistan is now going a step further by undergoing a state-centric ideological recalibration. This transformation does not yet match Saudi-style social liberalisation or the secular-nationalist transformation associated with Nasser’s Egypt. Pakistan is still struggling to find a clear direction. Its emerging model appears to combine Mohammed bin Salman’s state-controlled “moderate Islam”, the mutually reinforcing nationalism, military authority and state-regulated religious discourse of Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s Egypt, and Turkiye’s religious-conservative identity, nationalism and defence-industrial ambition. Briefly, the power elite wants religion to remain under state authority. It seeks a transition from transnational Islamic solidarity to the national interest; the creation of a modern, technologically capable Muslim state; religious scholars who support national cohesion rather than challenge statecraft or the ambitions of the ruling elite; and centralised control over security and foreign policy. However, the power elite also believes that the existing political order, governance model and constitutional arrangements obstruct the achievement of lasting stability. Interestingly, the Afghan Taliban, once close allies of Pakistan’s establishment, have taught it an important lesson: Islamist allies may possess their own nationalism, interests and territorial ambitions, which may not correspond with the vision of another country’s power elite. Middle powers with complicated neighbourhoods and significant defence capabilities often have additional strategic thoughts. They imagine renewed glory through alliances with friendly states possessing compatible capabilities and ambition. Major powers frequently exploit this tendency by encouraging middle powers to form alliances. Washington is encouraging the emerging defence architecture that has taken shape through the Makkah accord. China and Iran, meanwhile, are waiting for the US to reduce its regional footprint before revealing or advancing their own designs. The US and UK exploited this middle-power tendency several times during the Cold War. The Baghdad Pact was the most developed form of such an alliance. Established in the mid-1950s, it brought together Turkiye, Pakistan, Iraq, Iran and the UK. However, the project eventually collapsed due to internal upheavals in Iraq and Iran, and Turkiye also experienced domestic political instability. At that time, Pakistan was considered the alliance’s most stable regional partner, with politics largely under control and an economy that appeared to be flourishing. Pakistan’s power elite still dreams of returning to those days of perceived glory and reclaiming the country’s position among the leading middle powers of the Muslim world.
articles.author: Muhammad Amir Rana

articles.title: Meltdown in PCB
articles.content: ANYONE who has even casually followed Pakistan cricket over the years will know that our cricket board’s response tolosing the current Test series in Englandis a hysterical overreaction. After consecutive defeats at Headingley and Lord’s sealed the fate of the three-match rubber, the Pakistan Cricket Boardsackedthe head coach and fast-bowling coach, ordered seven players from the squad to pack their bags, and announced five novices and two recalls as their replacements. On top of that, one of the openers will be subjected to a disciplinary investigation for allegedly faking an injury. As actions of the PCB administration go, this is unprecedented. As human behaviour goes, this is lunacy. These developments have unleashed adeafening outrage, triggering embarrassing news headlines and sarcastic social media memes. That Pakistan’s cricket establishment has degenerated into such farce should come as no surprise. The PCB chairman has always been a handpicked political appointee — merit be damned. And since a fish rots from the head, there you have it. Yes, sometimes you will get lucky with the arrival of a Nur Khan or an Arif Abbasi at the helm, but these are fortuitous exceptions. A national cricket board chief is meant to be an elected official, voted in by representatives of regional cricket associations. This makes the position approachable and accountable. Instead, the practice in Pakistan is for the prime minister to dole out the PCB chairmanship as a favour or reward to an ally or acolyte. The typical outcome is whimsical and incompetent governance. Over time, this has resulted in a cricketing infrastructure that lacks the ability to identify, nurture and promote the best talent available. As actions of the PCB administration go, this is unprecedented. As human behaviour goes, this is lunacy. The one silver lining in this whole fiasco is that the ire of the cricket-following public has finally been deflected away from the players and squarely onto the PCB and its leadership. This is as it should be. We would normally have the players in our gunsights, as they are the most visible and hence the most obvious targets. But the blame ultimately lies elsewhere. To shine on the international stage, a cricketing tradition must rest on three pillars — an avid fan base, a rich talent pool, and a capable administration. There’s no question about the avidity of the fan base, nor about the richness of the talent pool. Just look at the whiplash that Pakistan’s cricket supporters go through with every victory and every defeat; that tells you all you need to know about their passionate commitment. As for talent, a country that has managed to produce all-time legends such as Javed Miandad, Zaheer Abbas, Wasim Akram, Waqar Younis and Younis Khan (among many others), is certainly not lacking in cricketing ability. That leaves governance and management, by far the most compromised pillar in Pakistan’s cricket edifice. It is honestly very hard to fathom what deliberations would have taken place in the upper echelons of the PCB that led to such a ridiculous knee-jerk outcome. It couldn’t have come from the high-performance director Aqib Javed, the lone international cricketer in PCB’s C-suite, because he would surely know better. Quite possibly Aqib might have advocated for a more measured approach. Yes, he has been staunchly defending the PCB’s actions in the media and on public forums, but the PCB command structure leaves him little choice. In all likelihood, the decision-making came solely from the PCB chief, Mr Mohsin Naqvi, himself. He may have asked for input from other bigwigs in the PCB’s corporate hierarchy, but none of them have any serious cricketing credentials. One can easily imagine them trying to guess what the boss wanted to hear, and then echoing it implicitly and explicitly. What thought process did Mohsin Naqvi undertake to do what he did? By the looks of it, not a very rigorous one. He is, to begin with, an overburdened man, holding the portfolio of federal minister for interior and narcotics control, in addition to his PCB hat. Moreover, he has emerged as a key member of the diplomatic team seeking peace in the Middle East, having visited Iran no less than six times since hostilities started. This mandate amounts to averting ‘World War III’, no small assignment. So we can reasonably conclude that Mr Naqvi as a cricket administrator is at best distracted, and at worst negligent. Meanwhile, there is still the issue of the cricket itself. Pakistan are scattered and scarred after losing the first two Tests. One can only imagine the terrified mood in the camp as the team anticipates the third and final Test, starting in Birmingham on Sept 9. Cricket is a funny game and a turnaround in Pakistani fortunes is theoretically possible, but the odds are of course heavily against it. The team is weak and demoralised, if not outright traumatised. Cricket fans have been left wondering if this is the worst Pakistani cricket outfit ever. It is worth remembering, however, that Pakistan cricket has seen much worse, both on and off the field. In 2002, in what is easily our worst Test scorecard ever, Pakistan faced Australia in a Test in Sharjah, totaling 59 in the first innings and 53 in the second, losing (naturally) by an innings — even though that team had included some great names. Then, in 2009, there was the terrorist attack outside Lahore’s Gaddafi Stadium that nearly killed the visiting Sri Lankan side. And in 2010 we had the spot-fixing disaster, which ended two highly promising fast-bowling careers and sent three Pakistani cricketers to London’s Crown Court, and thence to prison. Thankfully, we are now far removed from those catastrophes. The challenge ahead is to improve on-field performance and restore our international competitiveness. It won’t happen overnight, but if we can somehow manage to sort out the Gordian knot that is the Pakistan Cricket Board, that would make for an appropriate start to a revival of lost glory. The writer, a professor of neurology at Aga Khan University, has written on cricket for international publications.
articles.author: Saad Shafqat

articles.title: How many more?
articles.content: IN Pakistan, violence against women and girls is a human rights crisis. Hina Zareef was reportedly killed by her father for leaving an abusive and forced marriage. In another horrifying case, a woman was reportedly burned by her in-laws during a quarrel. Hina Javed was brutally murdered in her marital home. The reality is that, for many, a woman who asserts her autonomy is seen as someone who must be punished. Hina Zareef’s case was categorised by many as an ‘honour’-related crime. There is no honour in violence and control. Honour belongs to the woman, who had the immense courage to walk away from abuse, only to be killed by her own family. There have been several recent reports of violence against minor girls. A minor girl in Abbottabad was reportedly sexually assaulted at school, while the autopsy of a five-year-old from Haripur has revealed that she was raped. The rot in our society is deep. It is high time we recognise the scale and seriousness of the violence being inflicted and confront it with urgency. There must be an honest acknowledgement of rape culture in our society. Rape culture is reflected in the attitudes that justify violence, and the immediate instinct to question the victim. It is reflected in a society where we place great emphasis on controlling girls while failing to place the same emphasis on how boys are raised. It is sustained by the silence of other men who witness abusive behaviour but do not challenge it. It is reinforced by the drama industry that continues to portray controlling behaviour as romance and glamourises violence. For many, women asserting their autonomy must be punished. Many have advocated for the importance of sex education and conversations about consent as essential tools in challenging rape culture. It is crucial to teach children about bodily autonomy and the meaning of consent. That they have a right to say no and, equally, that they must respect another person’s no. When such conversations are treated as taboo, ignorance and harmful stereotypes take over. Despite passing anti-rape legislation, domestic violence laws, and amendments addressing ‘honour’ crimes, a severe gap exists between enactment and implementation. This is reflected in the dismal conviction rates in cases of gender-based violence. There is a lack of political will, and a judicial process that in many cases involves re-victimisation. Last year, the Lahore High Court held that where a valid marital bond continued to exist between a husband and wife, the husband could not be prosecuted for rape. Under the Hudood Ordinance, zina-bil-jabr (rape) was defined to exclude acts between individuals who were validly married. Subsequently, the Protection of Women (Criminal Laws Amendment) Act, 2006, introduced a revised definition of rape, and the marital rape exception was removed. Presently, the law no longer includes an exception for marital rape. If the legislature removed marriage as a barrier to a rape prosecution, the courts must not resurrect that exception. The most disturbing part of the ruling is it effectively treats marital status as a shield against allegations of sexual violence. In ‘Hassan Ahmed vs the State’, which is before the Supreme Court, the trial court and the high court convicted the accused for rape. The Supreme Court converted the conviction for rape into fornication. The Punjab government filed a review against this decision which was dismissed. As matters stand, the judiciary in Pakistan accepts that a case involving an alleged rape can be converted into fornication (even though fornication was not included as one of the offences in the charge). The court did not simply find the evidence insufficient to sustain a conviction for rape. It imputed consent and effectively treated the failure to establish rape as proof of consensual sexual intercourse. There is a fundamental difference between finding that there was insufficient evidence, and implying consent where the complainant has expressly stated that she did not consent. The Supreme Court went on to say that “the complainant is also liable to be proceeded against and punished as an accused of the offence of illicit intercourse with consent”. A woman who comes forward to report sexual violence should not have to fear that, if the prosecution fails to prove rape to the required standard, she herself may be put in the dock. In a society where fear, stigma and social consequences already silence countless victims, the risk of women being put on trial will only deepen that silence. Regrettably, dangerous stereotypes continue to persist in our jurisprudence: that the existence of a domestic or intimate relationship diminishes the allegations of violence, and that consent may be inferred from the circumstances rather than established as an express and voluntary choice. At every level, we are failing the victims.
articles.author: Rida Hosain

articles.title: Nobody’s job
articles.content: I STOOD in the immigration line at Jinnah International for 20 minutes and barely moved. Every counter was manned. Then they changed the officer at mine, and I was through in seven. Yes, I counted. The system was not broken. The system was fine. Last October, Omer and I returned to find chaos at immigration. It was everyone for themselves. The officer who eventually took my passport told me they had changed the system that day and none of them had got the hang of it yet. He looked exhausted. Two days before I flew out, the interior minister paid a surprise visit to this airport. He inspected the counters and asked passengers about their experience. While he was standing there, the immigration system went down. Mohsin Naqvi picked up the phone, called the relevant authorities and had it fixed. He then issued instructions that immigration should not stop under any circumstances, and that a backup should be in place for when the system fails. In April 2025, the Pakistan Airports Authority signed an agreement with a foreign consultancy to plan, design and install e-gates at Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi. A year later, the interior minister chaired a special meeting to review progress on the aforesaid installation, and also approved joint counters, a single-point screening system with the latest technology. The defence secretary also said that modern equipment was being imported to protect aircraft from bird strikes. A year between signing the contract and reviewing the progress and four months since that review, I walked through the same immigration without e-gates. The jokes write themselves here. I am trying not to make any. Look instead at what all of this has in common. Every item on the list is something to be bought: machinery, equipment, gates, and counters. None of it includes a decision about how many officers are on the desk at two in the morning, or about getting the passenger manifest into an officer’s hands before the aircraft has landed. The airport crisis is a failure of decisions. The FIA has published what it says it needs. On its own website, its immigration wing lists manual clearance instead of biometric processing, no access to the airline industry’s advance passenger information system, a shortage of manpower, and a lack of forgery detection equipment. Three of these are not purchases. They are arrangements. They require somebody to make a decision and then keep making it. So we buy things. That is the part of the problem we know how to solve. But look at what we won’t solve. The men with slips, walked to the front by airport staff who know exactly what they are doing. Nobody is embarrassed. Not the man, not the staff, not the officer who takes the passport out of turn. Everyone in that queue has watched it happen before. Behind them are men standing in the unaccompanied ladies’ line, and mothers carrying wailing babies with nowhere to sit. Imagine this is the first ‘face’ international travellers encounter when they land. By the time they leave, they will have fallen in love with the place. They will also have learned to expect this. Meanwhile, landing at an American airport’s long line is perhaps not as frustrating because one (at least me) is filled with anticipatory dread at which immigration officer you’ll get. But the queue was moving thanks to a woman directing people. Buy the machines by all means. Build the e-gates. But a gate does not decide how many counters open at two in the morning, and it does not notice when a queue has stopped moving. The woman at the American airport was not better at her job than anyone in Karachi. She had a job. Someone had looked at a hall full of people and decided that directing them was work worth paying for, and then kept paying for it. That is not a purchase. It is a decision, made once and renewed every day, and it is the cheapest item on the list. It was a young woman in line at Karachi airport who told off a man who was trying to sneak into a queue he was not allowed in. When the man tried to bulldoze his way, the immigration officer at the counter stepped out and told off all the men in that line. One was a poor young man who tried to explain that he was directed into that line by airline staff. The young woman didn’t realise she took it upon herself to do a job no one had assigned her. And it worked. Perhaps she should man (ha) the line at immigration. We won’t need ministers to make calls then. The writer is a journalist and conducts writing workshops in Karachi.
articles.author: Muna Khan

articles.title: Nourishing Pakistan
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S nutrition crisis is not short of diagnosis. What it lacks is the machinery and political discipline to act on what is known. That was the most useful message to emerge from DawnMedia’s two-day Act for Nutrition conference in Islamabad, where experts argued that malnutrition cannot be confined to the health sector. Over four in 10 children under five are stunted, while the economic cost of malnutrition is estimated at $17bn annually. Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal’s promise that the Planning Commission will take ownership of nutrition and early childhood development is therefore significant. It recognises that this is a human-capital and development crisis involving health, agriculture, education, water, sanitation, population policy and social protection. Speakers also stressed that 30pc to 40pc of stunting occurs before birth, making maternal nutrition, antenatal care, birth spacing and the first 1,000 days of life critical. Adolescence, too, cannot remain the forgotten interval between childhood and motherhood. Equally important was the emphasis on water and sanitation. Feeding a child better will achieve little if contaminated water and repeated infection undermine growth. Calls for targeted WASH investment in high-burden districts should be taken seriously. The problem is that Pakistan has heard much of this before. Policies exist, programmes operate and donor money flows, yet nutrition remains fragmented among institutions that rarely plan, finance or deliver together. The Benazir Nashonuma Programme shows that progress is possible. Children enrolled in it were found to be 22pc less likely to be stunted at six months. The challenge is to connect such interventions with primary healthcare, family planning, clean water, sanitation and local social services, rather than treating each as a separate scheme. The conference’s proposal to regard nutrition spending as capital investment rather than simply health expenditure is also worth pursuing. Preventing stunting is investment in future learning, productivity and national income. But declarations must now give way to measurable commitments. Pakistan still relies on the 2018 National Nutrition Survey for its headline 40.2pc stunting figure, an extraordinary data gap for a crisis repeatedly described as a national emergency. A fresh national survey, dedicated budget lines, provincial and district targets, named officials responsible for delivery and regular public reporting should be the minimum next steps. Recognising food and nutritional security as a basic right may strengthen the framework, but rights without budgets and accountability remain promises on paper. Pakistan knows how malnutrition comes about and what can reduce it. The failure is no longer one of knowledge. It is the state’s failure to organise itself around the child. The conference has sharpened the diagnosis. Government must now prove it can deliver.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Climate test
articles.content: THE world is edging into climate territory governments have spent years trying to avoid. A new UN Environment Programme reportwarnsthat the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C warming threshold is likely to be breached within the next few years. That does not mean climate action has failed or that the target no longer matters. UNEP argues that humanity must keep any “overshoot” as low and brief as possible, as every fraction of warming raises the risk of extreme weather, ecosystem loss and irreversible tipping points. Adding to the concern, the World Meteorological Organisation says theEl Niño strengtheningin the Pacific could be the strongest in four decades, intensifying heat, drought and floods worldwide. For Pakistan, the fallout could include water stress, food insecurity and greater strain on urban infrastructure and services. TheNepal-China floodshave shown how quickly climate hazards can devastate lives. As warming intensifies, Pakistan will increasingly have to contend with several climate stresses at once, often in places least equipped to cope. That demands a rethink of how the country plans for development. Pakistan must plan for a climate changing faster than its institutions. Adaptation cannot remain confined to emergency response after floods, heatwaves or droughts. Development policy itself must change. New housing, roads, power systems and urban drainage should be built for harsher weather. Water policy must account for uncertain river flows and rainfall. Agriculture needs crops and irrigation methods better suited to greater heat and water stress, along with support to help farmers adapt. Cities require heat-action plans, shaded public spaces and stronger protection for outdoor workers. A World Bank assessment covering Pakistan and the wider MENAAP region found that prolonged extreme heat is depressing sales, labour productivity and wages, showing that climate damage is also an economic competitiveness problem. None of this absolves the major emitters. UNEP identifies finance, equity and global cooperation as essential to navigating a dangerous climate future, while stressing that countries with greater responsibility for global warming must act fastest. Pakistan should press that case. But it must also spend development resources intelligently. The age of treating climate disasters as one-off emergencies has ended and it must plan for a harsher reality.
articles.author: Editorial
